# School Ethnic Density and Mental Health Problems in Black, Latine, and White Preadolescent Children

**Authors:** Saúl Urbina-Johanson; Natalie Slopen; Seetha Davis; Scott Delaney; Henning Tiemeier

**Affiliations:** aHarvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts | bHarvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

## Abstract

Previous studies suggest school ethnic density is associated with less internalizing problems in Black and Latine adolescents in high school. Here, we assessed associations between school ethnic density and internalizing, externalizing, and thought problems in Black, Latine, and White pre-adolescent children (mean age=9.9 years) in elementary school. We additionally examined if associations differed by family generational status.

We analyzed baseline data from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study (n=10, 076). We operationalized school ethnic density as a measure of racial and/or ethnic concordance. In models stratified by race and ethnicity, we used generalized estimating equation models to assess associations between proportions of school racial and/or ethnic concordance and the internalizing, externalizing, and thought problem subscales of the Child Behavior Checklist. We subsequently adjusted for family and neighborhood socioeconomic factors and tested for interactions with family generational status.

For Black children, a higher proportion of Black students at schools was associated with less internalizing (β=−1.11, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): −2.82, −.13; p =.026) and thought problems (β=−.47, 95% CI: −.78, −.06; p =.026). For Latine children, a higher proportion of Latine students was associated with less thought problems, but only among children from immigrant families (β=−.65, 95% CI: −1.20, −.09; p =.023). For White children, an initial association between a higher proportion of White students and less externalizing problems disappeared after controlling for socioeconomic factors.

We find protective associations between school ethnic density and mental health problems for Black children and Latine children from immigrant families.

Associations between School Ethnic Density and Psychopathology Symptoms among Black, Latine, and White Children in the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study; https://osf.io/3rh74.

## INTRODUCTION

In the United States (U.S.), Black and Hispanic/Latine (henceforth referred to as Latine) children are more likely than White children to attend socioeconomically disadvantaged schools that offer fewer academically enriching opportunities.1–3 Inequities in school contexts have been shown to contribute to racial and ethnic inequities in educational attainment and physical health.4,5 In hopes of mitigating these inequities, many policies have sought to create more racially and ethnically diverse schools, some of which have been shown to significantly improve the educational attainment and physical health of Black and Latine individuals.6–8 However, recent studies have also found that Black and Latine children tend to experience worse mental health in schools with more White students and fewer students of their shared racial and/or ethnic background, despite the socioeconomic advantages of these schools.9 These findings align with the ethnic density hypothesis, which posits that racial and ethnic minorities derive mental health benefits from spaces with higher ethnic density; that is, spaces with relatively more individuals of other minoritized racial or ethnic backgrounds or their same racial or ethnic background.10 While findings have generally supported this hypothesis, results vary across groups, countries, and mental health outcomes. For example, a study within the United Kingdom found no differences in general mental health associated with higher neighborhood ethnic density for minoritized adolescents.11 For Black and Latine youth within the U.S., higher ethnic density at the school level has been found to predict lower internalizing problems, but higher ethnic density at the neighborhood level has been found to predict both lower internalizing problems and lower risk for psychosis.12–16 While similar patterns have been found with neighborhood ethnic density and externalizing problems, the evidence is mixed.17

In this pre-registered analysis (osf.io/3rh74) of Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study data, we assessed whether school ethnic density was associated with internalizing, externalizing, and thought problems in non-Latine Black (henceforth referred to as Black), Latine, and non-Latine White (henceforth referred to as White) pre-adolescent children attending elementary school in the U.S. Specifically, we operationalized school ethnic density as a measure of racial and/or ethnic concordance (henceforth referred to as ethnic concordance), the proportion of students enrolled at a school who were of the same racial and/or ethnic background as a given child.

Several recent studies from the National Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (AddHealth) in the U.S. found that attending schools with higher proportions of White students is associated with a more negative self-image for Black and Latine late adolescents and more depressive symptoms for Black late adolescents.13, 18 Similarly, a study based in 14 schools across Texas found higher depression scores for Black and Latine children attending schools with higher proportions of White students.12 However, to date, only one study from the U.S. has operationalized school ethnic density with a measure of ethnic concordance.14 This study, conducted by Hargrove 2023, used AddHealth data to find that Black late adolescents in schools with higher proportions of Black students had lower depression scores, with the effects being most pronounced for those of darker skin tones.

Importantly, significant heterogeneity exists within racial and ethnic groups. Overlapping identities, such as those related to skin color, gender, and sexual orientation, influence the way children experience the world and likely the ethnic density of their environments. A critical source of intergroup heterogeneity is family generational status, how long a child and their family have resided in the U.S. Prior studies of neighborhood ethnic density in Europe and Canada have found ethnic density to have protective mental health effects for recent immigrants.19,20 One population-based cohort study of immigrants from Africa and the Middle East in Denmark found the protective effects of neighborhood ethnic density on the incidence of psychosis to be specific to second-generation immigrants and absent for first-generation immigrants.21 To our knowledge, no study has assessed interactions with family generational status in the association between school ethnic density and mental health in the U.S. Compared to children from U.S.-born families, children from immigrant families may be more exposed to stressors related to acculturation and exclusionary immigration policies, both of which may be eased by higher ethnic density. However, evidence suggests children from immigrant families have a stronger ethnic racial identity, a sense of belonging to a racial and/or ethnic group that is protective against mental health problems.22,23 High ethnic density schools, and perhaps especially high ethnic concordance schools, may promote ethnic racial identity development in children from U.S.-born families, who may still experience stressors related to being a U.S. minority without the protective effects of a higher ethnic racial identity. As such, while the protective effects of ethnic density may be present for children from immigrant families, they may be present and stronger for children from U.S.-born families.

Here, we used data from the ABCD Study to fill four existing gaps in the literature. First, we assessed associations between school ethnic density and mental health using a school-level measure of ethnic concordance. Second, we focused on Black, Latine, and White pre-adolescent children, a critical developmental window when mental health problems tend to emerge. Indeed, while previous studies have found associations between school ethnic density and mental health problems in late adolescence, these patterns may exist earlier. We hypothesized a protective association between school ethnic density and mental health problems, where higher proportions of ethnic concordance would be associated with less internalizing, externalizing, and thought problems, a developmental risk factor for psychotic symptoms.24 Given the suggested mechanisms linking ethnic density and mental health, we hypothesized that these associations would be specific to Black and Latine children. Third, we carefully controlled for socioeconomic status at the family and neighborhood levels. Most studies on school ethnic density and mental health have controlled for socioeconomic status at the school level, but substantial evidence suggests socioeconomic factors at the family and neighborhood levels are likely to directly influence both children’s mental health and their school environments.25,26 Fourth, we assessed interactions between school ethnic density and family generational status. We hypothesized that family generational status would modify associations between school ethnic density and mental health outcomes for Black and Latine children, with ethnic concordance displaying a larger protective association for children from U.S.-born families than for children from immigrant families.

## METHOD

### Participants

ABCD is a longitudinal study of neurobehavioral development and child health. Between 2016 and 2018, children ages 9 and 10 were recruited from 21 sites across the U.S. An epidemiologically informed recruitment strategy was used to closely mirror the demographic and socioeconomic makeup of the U.S.27

For our cross-sectional analyses, we used baseline data from 11,868 participants. Data were limited to Black, Latine, and White participants (N =11,337). Participants of other racial and ethnic backgrounds were excluded (N = 531) due to small sample sizes. Given a-priori hypotheses that different racial and ethnic groups would display unique associations with school ethnic concordance, all analyses were stratified by participants’ race and/or ethnicity (i.e., Black, Latine, and White).

Participants were excluded if they were missing data on school ethnic concordance (described below) (N =1,255) or mental health outcomes (N = 6) (i.e., 10–15% of each racial and/or ethnic group). This left 10,076 participants: 2,049 Black children, 2,224 Latine children, and 5,803 White children. Our study used ABCD data from the 5.0 data release. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board at each ABCD site. Caregivers provided informed consent and children provided assent.

### Measures

#### Racial and ethnic identity.

We conceptualize race and ethnicity as social constructs that impact the lived experience of children in the U.S. When completing a demographics questionnaire, participants’ caregivers were able to select multiple racial and ethnic groups for their child(ren). To prevent overlap across groups, participants of any race who were identified as Latine were placed in the Latine group (N = 2,224). Within the Latine group, N = 1,523 participants were identified as White and N = 195 as Black. Non-Latine participants were placed in the Black or White group. Participants identified as Black and White were placed in the Black group (N = 388).

#### School ethnic concordance.

We measured school ethnic concordance, our operationalization of school ethnic density, as the proportion of students within a school of the same race or ethnicity as a given participant. Data were obtained from the Stanford Education Data Archive (SEDA, version 4.1), a dataset linked to ABCD that contains the proportion of students within each school who identify as Black, Hispanic [Latine], and White, according to the Common Core of Data (CCD), summarized as the weighted averages from 2009 to 2018 for each school. Additional details are available elsewhere.28 From the SEDA, we constructed an alternate measure of school ethnic density for sensitivity analyses: the proportion non-White students within each school.

#### Mental health problems.

We used scores from the internalizing, externalizing, and thought problems scales of the school-age version of the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) (6–18, parent-report), a reliable and valid instrument consisting of 113 questions assessing mental health problems in children and adolescents.29 Raw scores were used to preserve natural variation in the data.

#### Family generational status.

Participants’ caregivers provided information about the country of birth of their child, their child’s biological mother and biological father, and their child’s maternal and paternal grandparents. Child’s generational status was coded as 4th+ generation if no biological parents or grandparents were born outside of the U.S.; 3rd generation if at least one of their grandparents was born outside of the U.S.; 2nd generation if either of their parents was born outside of the U.S.; and 1st generation if the participant was born outside of the U.S. Due to sample size limitations and to capture differences in children’s proximity to the immigrant experience, 1st and 2nd generation participants were grouped as children from immigrant families and 3rd and 4th+ generation participants as children from U.S.-born families.

#### Covariates.

The following covariates were selected as potential confounders: child’s sex assigned at birth, child age, maternal age, family income to needs ratio (i.e., family gross income divided by the federal poverty level relative to household size), and household highest level of education. Additionally, we adjusted for the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) based on the participant’s residential address at baseline.30 The ADI is an external variable linked to ABCD designed to capture overall levels of socioeconomic disadvantage at the census block group level. Finally, derived from SEDA, we included a variable to indicate whether a participant’s school was a regular versus alternative school.

### Statistical Analyses

All analyses were conducted with R (version 4.0). Generalized estimating equation models were run using the R package ‘geepack’ to examine associations between proportions of ethnic concordance and three mental health outcomes (i.e., internalizing, externalizing, and thought problems) in separate models. To examine the role of socioeconomic variables, two sets of models were run. The first set included covariates of child sex, child age, maternal age, family generational status, and school type. The second set additionally included socioeconomic variables at the family and neighborhood levels: family income to needs ratio, household highest level of education, and the ADI. We did not control for socioeconomic status at the school level because of the causal structure between school and neighborhood socioeconomic status, with most schools within the U.S. being heavily influenced by neighborhood characteristics.26

To test for effect modification by family generational status, we replicated our second set of models with the addition of an interaction term (i.e., school ethnic concordance * family generational status). When the interaction term was significant, models were further stratified by family generational status.

For optimal generalized equation modeling, we selected a gaussian family and an exchangeable correlation structure. These were selected to be maximally valid in the event of model misspecification. Because of the presence of twins and siblings in the ABCD sample, we clustered participants within families. Due to R code limitations with multilevel clustering, research site was added as a fixed effect. School identification variables were not included because they were unavailable for baseline data, with over two-thirds of data missing.

Missing covariates were imputed using multiple imputation models with 20 imputed datasets (‘mice’ package). Percentages of missing data are noted in Table 1. After generating 20 imputed datasets, we performed the analyses within each imputed dataset and combined the results using Rubin’s rule.31

Statistical tests of hypotheses were 2-tailed, with the significance level set at a p-value of less than .05.

## RESULTS

### Sample Demographics

Table 1 outlines the demographics of our final analytical sample, stratified into three groups. Of note, the distribution of family generational status was most even within the Latine group; approximately 60% of Latine children were from immigrant families and 40% from U.S.-born families. In contrast, more than 85% of children within the Black and White groups were from U.S.-born families. Black and Latine children were, on average, of lower socioeconomic status than White children.

### Mental Health Problems across Racial, Ethnic, and Generational Groups

As detailed in Table 2, internalizing problems were highest among Latine children; externalizing problems were highest among Black children; and thought problems were highest among White children. For all groups, internalizing, externalizing, and thought problems were higher for children from U.S.-born families than for children from immigrant families. Table 3 additionally shows unadjusted correlations between the racial and ethnic composition of schools and mental health problems.

### Associations between School Ethnic Concordance and Mental Health Problems in Black, Latine, and White Children

For Black children, results from Model 1 showed associations between higher school ethnic concordance and less internalizing problems (β = −1.36, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) −2.28, .44;, p =.004) and thought problems (β = −.47, 95%CI −.86, −.07; p =.021) (see Table 4); there was no association between ethnic concordance and externalizing problems (β = .05, 95%CI −1.0,1.1; p =.922). When controlling for socioeconomic variables in Model 2, these associations remained present for internalizing problems (β = −1.11, 95%CI −2.82, −.13; p =.026) and thought problems (β = −.47, 95%CI −.78,−.06; p =.026) and absent for externalizing problems (β = −.28, 95%CI −1.43, .86; p =.629). For Latine children, Model 1 and Model 2 results showed no associations between school ethnic concordance and internalizing, externalizing, or thought problems. For White children, results from Model 1 showed associations between higher ethnic concordance and less externalizing problems (β = −1.38, 95%CI −2.27, −.500; p =.002) and thought problems (β = −.40, 95%CI −.72, −.09; p =.013). There was no association between ethnic concordance and internalizing problems (β = .50, 95%CI −1.28, .28; p =.212). When controlling for socioeconomic variables in Model 2, all associations between school ethnic concordance and mental health problems disappeared for White children. See Tables S1−S9, available online, for full models.

### Effect Modification by Family Generational Status

Interaction terms between school ethnic concordance and family generational status were included in models controlling for socioeconomic variables. An interaction was found for Latine children in the association with externalizing problems (p = .013) and thought problems (p = .015) (See Figures S1 and S2, available online, for Johnson-Neyman plots). Interaction terms were not significant (p > .05) for internalizing problems for Latine children and all mental health outcomes for Black and White children.

Latine children were further stratified into children from immigrant families and children from U.S.-born families. Adjusted models were re-run within these strata for externalizing problems and thought problems, as well as internalizing problems to contrast results. Higher ethnic concordance was associated with less thought problems, but only for Latine children from immigrant families (β = −.65, 95%CI −1.20,−.09; p =.023; see Table 5).

### Sensitivity Analyses

Three sensitivity analyses were run. 1) Multiracial Black and White children within the Black group were removed from analyses (N = 388). 2) All models were re-run using ABCD’s construction of a race-ethnicity variable, which differs from ours in that it excludes multiracial children from its Black and White groups. The magnitude and direction of all associations remained for these two sensitivity analyses, but the estimates were less precise due to the smaller sample sizes, particularly for the Black group (see Tables S10–S12, available online). 3) All models were re-run using an alternate measure of school ethnic density, the proportion of non-White students enrolled at schools. Effects across both measures of ethnic density were similar for Black and White children but diverged for Latine children (see Tables S13 and S14, available online). First, interactions between ethnic density and family generational status were only significant for externalizing problems in Latine children. Second, higher proportions of non-White students were associated with more externalizing problems for Latine children from U.S.-born families (β = 2.16, 95%CI .075, 4.23; p =.042).

## DISCUSSION

In this pre-registered analysis of ABCD data, we found protective associations between higher ethnic density at the school level and children’s mental health. As hypothesized, the associations were specific to Black and Latine children. Indeed, we observed associations between higher school ethnic density, measured as ethnic concordance, and less internalizing and thought problems for Black children. Similarly, we observed an association between higher school ethnic concordance and less thought problems for Latine children, but only for those from immigrant families. Among White children, initial analyses displayed an association between higher school ethnic concordance and less externalizing problems; however, this association disappeared after adjusting for socioeconomic status at family and neighborhood levels. While our cross-sectional design prevents us from drawing causal inferences, our pattern of results suggests that ethnic density at the school level may confer protective effects on the mental health of Black and first- and second-generation Latine children in the U.S., particularly for internalizing and thought problems.

In numerous ways, our study contributes to the growing body of evidence linking ethnic density at the school level in the U.S. with children’s mental health. Previous studies have found that higher proportions of White students in schools are associated with more internalizing problems among Black adolescents.12,13,18 Our study extends upon these findings by using an alternate measure of school ethnic density, ethnic concordance, to conversely predict less internalizing problems among Black children. We expand further upon past findings by assessing the association of school ethnic concordance with two other types of mental health problems: externalizing and thought problems. One previous study in the U.S. linked higher proportions of racial and ethnic minorities at the neighborhood level with remission of psychosis risk symptoms among non-White adolescents at clinically high risk for psychosis.16 To our knowledge, our study is the first to link higher ethnic concordance at the school level with less thought problems, a developmental risk factor for psychosis, in Black children and Latine children from immigrant families, while rigorously controlling for socioeconomic factors at family and neighborhood levels. Importantly, the thought problems subscale of the CBCL combines a wide range of behaviors that may signal risk for other syndromes in addition to psychosis.

Together, our findings highlight how Black, Latine, and White children may differently experience ethnic density at the school level, with higher school ethnic concordance only being associated with less internalizing and thought problems for Black children and less thought problems for Latine children from immigrant families. These group differences may suggest that internalizing and thought problems are more influenced by stressors commonly experienced by racial and ethnic minorities, such as discrimination and other forms of interpersonal racism. In contrast, externalizing problems, particularly in White children, may be more influenced by socioeconomic factors that are related to the racial and ethnic makeup of schools. While our study does not delve into the mechanisms linking ethnic concordance to lower risk for different mental health problems across these groups, future research should explore these to enhance our understanding of the etiology of various disorders and improve public health prevention efforts. These mechanisms may include a lower likelihood of experiencing interpersonal racism and increased feelings of social support, cohesion, and belonging.32,33 Additionally, these may include structural exposures, such as a stronger embedding of racial and ethnic cultural programming, less punitive discipline strategies, or a makeup of the staff that is more diverse or more racially and/or ethnically concordant with a child’s identity. Furthermore, the mechanisms may differ depending on how ethnic density is operationalized, with measures of ethnic concordance more likely reflecting protective factors than measures of schools’ proportions of non-White students. This may explain the slight differences between our main analyses and our third sensitivity analysis, which suggest measures of ethnic concordance and proportions of non-White students may not always be used interchangeably.

Our study highlights points of divergence not only across the groups of Black, Latine, and White children, but also within them. We specifically find that family generation status interacts with ethnic density at the school level among Latine children, where higher school ethnic concordance was associated with less thought problems, but only among children from immigrant families. This finding warrants further investigation, as multiple complex mechanisms are likely involved. For instance, Latine children from immigrant families may benefit from higher ethnic concordance in schools due to reduced language barriers. These children may also benefit because their caregivers can more easily participate in school activities, potentially building connections with other parents and learning to navigate various challenges in the absence of access to social safety net programs. In contrast, children and families who have resided in the U.S. for a longer period may not rely as heavily on high ethnic concordance environments, perhaps due to their greater English proficiency and increased access to social safety net programs. Whatever the case, our finding is particularly novel given that most of the literature on ethnic density uses categories of race and ethnicity based on the U.S. Census or other national designators. While this approach greatly advances our knowledge of how different racial and ethnic groups experience ethnic density, prior research documents its limitations.34 Namely, using this approach, we overlook significant heterogeneity within broad social categories of race and ethnicity. Consistent with intersectionality theory, it is important to examine factors that interact with race and ethnicity, such as family generational status, to differently shape experiences and health outcomes within and across groups.

Our results contradict our hypotheses in two ways. First, we hypothesized that school ethnic concordance would exhibit a stronger protective association for children from U.S.-born families than for children from immigrant families. However, a protective association was only found for children from immigrant families, specifically regarding thought problems in Latine children. While contrary to our hypotheses, these results are consistent with research from Europe and Canada that finds protective effects of neighborhood ethnic density on risk for psychosis among recent adult immigrants.19,20 Future research should investigate the specific characteristics of these high ethnic density contexts that contribute to reducing the risk for psychosis for recent immigrants. However, as it is possible that we were underpowered to detect group differences in effect sizes, future research should also make use of larger samples to replicate, expand upon, or contrast our results.

Second, we hypothesized that an interaction between school ethnic concordance and family generational status would be present for both Black and Latine children. However, an interaction was only present for Latine children. This specificity may suggest that the stressors faced by Black children are not as sensitive to differences in family generational status as the stressors faced by Latine children. Alternatively, this specificity may also be due to differences in statistical power. Our group of Black children mostly consisted of children from U.S.-born families, which impacted our ability to examine differences in the associations with mental health by generational status. Therefore, future research should investigate these interactions in samples of Black children from more varied family generational status backgrounds.

Our study has limitations. First, its cross-sectional design. ABCD provides repeating measures for mental health problems, but not for school ethnic concordance. Therefore, we were unable to pursue a longitudinal design. Employing dynamic measures of school ethnic concordance and children’s mental health over longitudinal designs, as well as drawing on data from natural experiments (e.g., bussing, school lotteries), could enhance causal inference in future studies. Second, due to sample size constraints, our analyses were restricted to Black, Latine, and White children. This restriction limits the generalizability of our findings to other minoritized racial and/or ethnic groups, who may be sensitive to ethnic concordance in divergent ways. Third, due to small sample sizes, we were similarly unable to assess how multiracial and/or multiethnic children potentially differently experience school ethnic density. Fourth, not all ABCD participants could be included due to missing data for school ethnic concordance. However, there were no major differences found between participants included in and excluded from our final sample (see Table S15, available online). Fifth, we were unable to cluster our data at the school level given the high level of missing school identification variables. Sixth, we categorized children into racial and/or ethnic groups according to the U.S. Census. While these categories are commonly used, significant heterogeneity exists within them, and many individuals may not identify with the racial or ethnic group socially assigned to them within the U.S. context.35,36 Seventh, although our separate models revealed divergent associations between school ethnic concordance and different mental health problems, they increased the possibility of Type 1 errors, as prior research suggests that different types of mental health problems co-occur and influence one another.37

The study has several strengths. It is the first study of ethnic density at the school level in the U.S. to use the SEDA, a structural measure of the racial and ethnic demographics of schools across the country. Previous studies have aggregated individual-level data into a school-level measure. This method is subject to confounding, as the sample participating in the study influences the overall measure of the school environment. Our study makes use of the SEDA, which was constructed independently from our sample, to bypass the limitations of this method. Second, we use a structural measure of the school environment to assess its relationship with children’s mental health. Prior ABCD studies have used questionnaires that assess children’s subjective experience of their school environment.38,39 This method is subject to reverse causation or the common method bias, as individuals with worse mental health may more negatively assess their school environment.40 Moreover, structural measures can capture aspects of children’s experiences that are more difficult to assess by questionnaires or that perhaps go beyond the conscious awareness of developing children. Third, whereas most literature on ethnic density is with adolescents and adults, our study examines associations between school ethnic density and mental health in younger children within a developmental period when mental health problems begin to emerge.

In summary, our findings provide evidence for protective effects of ethnic density at the school level for Black children and Latine children from immigrant families in the U.S. Notably, we find that these effects are specific to internalizing and thought problems. We encourage future researchers to identify what characteristics of high ethnic density environments decrease risk for mental health problems in minoritized children. In addition to identifying the characteristics of these environments that contribute to decreased risk for mental health problems, it is important for future research to delineate the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms that mediate risk to these specific types of mental health problems. Critically, while we included family generational status as an effect modifier to attempt to uncover heterogeneity within racial and/or ethnic groups, many other identity characteristics may warrant investigation, including sex, gender, sexual orientation, and language spoken at home.

School ethnic concordance is also one factor among many to examine in the study of school demographics and mental health. We focus on racial and ethnic demographics given their complex, historical interaction with socioeconomic factors within the U.S. However, a critical area for future inquiry is to assess how other school demographics, such as gender in all-male or all-female schools, may similarly moderate risk or protection for mental health problems. Historically, many education opportunity interventions seeking to better support racially and ethnically minoritized youth have been single-gendered.41

To close, our study is focused only on mental health outcomes, which should be considered in tandem with other important outcomes, such as academic, economic, and physical health trajectories. Our study found mental health benefits of ethnic density at a school level, but these findings must be contextualized with the current state of the education system in the U.S., where Black and Latine children are more likely than White children to attend schools that are underperforming academically. This knowledge has prompted efforts to improve integration (e.g., bussing programs and school choice) to improve academic outcomes. While this may indeed improve academic outcomes for Black and Latine children, it is important to consider that this seemingly positive result may be only “skin deep resilience,” where these children must overcome significantly different challenges in these new environments that facilitate their academic success but perhaps at a cost to their mental health.42 Therefore, in contexts of lower ethnic density, policies and interventions to foster mental health may function by fostering inclusion, recruiting diverse faculty, as well as by decreasing discrimination and bullying on the basis of race or ethnicity.

## Data Sharing:

Data is already currently available through NDA at NIH as part of the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. Interested parties can request the data here: https://nda.nih.gov/abcd/request-access.

Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (https://abcdstudy.org), held in the NIMH Data Archive (NDA). This is a multisite, longitudinal study designed to recruit more than 10,000 children age 9–10 and follow them over 10 years into early adulthood. A listing of participating sites and a complete listing of the study investigators can be found at https://abcdstudy.org/consortium_members/. ABCD consortium investigators designed and implemented the study and/or provided data but did not necessarily participate in the analysis or writing of this report. This manuscript reflects the views of the authors and may not reflect the opinions or views of the NIH or ABCD consortium investigators. The ABCD data repository grows and changes over time. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study is an open-access database and can be accessed at https://abcdstudy.org, held in the NIMH Data Archive. Data can be accessed following a data request to the NIH data access committee (https://nda.nih.gov/), which should include information on the planned topic of study. The following data sets were generated under NIMH Data Archive: [School Ethnic Density and Mental Health Problems in Black, Latine, and White Pre-Adolescent Children in the United States; DOI: 10.15154/1kgb-qs53].
